Chapter 6
Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)

This document replaces Chapter 6 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (2020), book pages 163 to 192 (PDF pages 221 to 250). It follows the book's order, keeps its learning objectives, and adds plain-English explanations, command breakdowns, labs and questions. Every difference from the book is tagged so you can see what is original and what is not.

Write your answer on paper first. Then mark your confidence: K (I know it), U (unsure), G (I guessed). Answers are in Answer Key A at the end. Be honest: this is how the tracker stays honest.
Q1. What is the default administrative distance of OSPF? (Confidence: K / U / G)
Q2. Two routers are in the same area, but one sends Hellos every 10 seconds and the other every 5 seconds. Will they become neighbors? (Confidence: K / U / G)
Q3. What is the wildcard mask for a /27 network? (Confidence: K / U / G)
Q4. A router has the command router-id 9.9.9.9 and also a loopback 0 with address 1.1.1.1. Which one is the router ID? (Confidence: K / U / G)
Q5. Three routers on one Ethernet segment have default priorities and router IDs 1.1.1.1, 2.2.2.2 and 3.3.3.3. All start together. Which router becomes the DR? (Confidence: K / U / G)

The idea in plain words. OSPF is a link-state routing protocol. Every router in an area learns the full map of that area (who is connected to whom). Each router then runs the SPF (Dijkstra) algorithm on that map to find the best path to every network, and puts those paths in its routing table. This is different from RIP, where routers only pass around distances and never see the map. BOOK p164
Why people like OSPF [BOOK]
- Open standard: works between vendors (but see the warning on cost later).
- Fast convergence, and it supports equal-cost multipath (several equal best routes).
- Supports VLSM / CIDR and has no hop-count limit.
- Sends updates only when something changes (event-triggered) and uses areas to keep updates small.
- Supports IPv4 (OSPFv2) and IPv6 (OSPFv3, a separate version of the protocol).
OSPF compared with RIP (book Table 6.1) [BOOK] p165
| Characteristic | OSPF | RIPv2 | RIPv1 |
| Type of protocol | Link state | Distance vector | Distance vector |
| Classless / VLSM | Yes | Yes | No |
| Auto-summarization | No | Yes | Yes |
| Manual summarization | Yes | Yes | No |
| Route propagation | Multicast on change | Periodic multicast | Periodic broadcast |
| Path metric | Cost (based on bandwidth) | Hops | Hops |
| Hop count limit | None | 15 | 15 |
| Convergence | Fast | Slow | Slow |
| Hierarchy (areas) | Yes | No | No |
| Route computation | Dijkstra (SPF) | Bellman-Ford | Bellman-Ford |
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
The book's text under the table says "Table 4.1". It means Table 6.1. This is a typo in the book. UPDATED
Areas and the two special routers [BOOK] p166
- Area: a group of contiguous networks and routers that share the same map. Areas cut routing overhead, speed up convergence and keep a problem inside one area.
- Area 0 (backbone): every other area must connect to area 0 (virtual links are outside this book).
- ABR (area border router): a router with interfaces in more than one area. At least one interface must be in area 0.
- ASBR (autonomous system boundary router): a router that connects the OSPF network to an outside routing domain.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

The book says OSPF "absolutely must have an area 0". That is true for multi-area designs. A single-area OSPF network will work in any area number, but use area 0 anyway. The exam uses single-area OSPF, and area 0 is the safe habit. ADDED CHECK
Quick check 6.1
Q1. Which algorithm does OSPF use to calculate best paths?
Answer: SPF (Dijkstra) - RIP uses Bellman-Ford.
Q2. What is the name of a router that has interfaces in two different OSPF areas?
Answer: ABR - Area border router.
Q3. Does OSPF send periodic full routing-table updates like RIPv1?
Answer: No - OSPF sends event-triggered updates (LSAs) when the topology changes.
Q4. Why use areas?
Answer: To reduce routing overhead, speed convergence, and contain instability - These are the three reasons the book gives.
6.1.1 OSPF Terminology
You must know these terms before the commands make sense. Read the table slowly; then say each term out loud in your own words. BOOK pp167-169
| Term | Plain meaning |
| Link | An interface added to OSPF. It has an up/down state and IP address(es). |
| Router ID (RID) | A 32-bit number written like an IPv4 address. It is the "name" of the router in OSPF. Chosen as shown in section 6.3. |
| Neighbor | Another OSPF router on the same link that you have seen Hellos from, with matching settings. |
| Adjacency | A neighbor you have gone further with: you exchange full databases with it. Not every neighbor becomes adjacent. |
| DR (designated router) | Elected on broadcast links. Everyone else forms adjacency with the DR so the number of adjacencies stays small. |
| BDR (backup DR) | A hot standby for the DR on the same link. |
| Hello protocol | Finds neighbors and keeps the relationship alive. Hellos go to 224.0.0.5. |
| Neighbor table | List of routers you have seen Hellos from (show ip ospf neighbor). |
| Topology database (LSDB) | All LSAs received for the area. The input to SPF (show ip ospf database). |
| LSA | Link State Advertisement: a packet that describes links and routes. Only shared with adjacent routers. |
| Area | A group of routers and networks with the same area ID and the same map. |
| Broadcast (multi-access) | Ethernet-style link: many devices, broadcast works. DR and BDR are elected. |
| NBMA | Many devices, no broadcast (old Frame Relay, X.25, ATM). Needs special configuration. |
| Point-to-point | Exactly two routers on the link. No DR or BDR. |
| Point-to-multipoint | One interface to many routers, all on one subnet. Special OSPF configuration. |
EXAM CRITICAL
Neighbors must match on: area ID, stub area flag, authentication (if used), and Hello and Dead intervals. BOOK p167

Also needed, but not in the book: the two interfaces must be in the same subnet with the same mask on broadcast links, the network types must be compatible, and the router IDs must be different. ADDED
COMMON MISTAKE

The book says Hello packets and LSAs "build and maintain the topological database". Only LSAs build the database. Hellos find and keep neighbors. UPDATED (RFC 2328 describes the Hello protocol for neighbor discovery and the LSAs for the database.)
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's NBMA examples (Frame Relay, X.25, ATM) are old technology. On the exam, concentrate on broadcast (Ethernet) and point-to-point links. NBMA and point-to-multipoint are not named in the objectives. UPDATED
DR and BDR election: the rules [ADDED]
- Only on broadcast (and NBMA) links. Point-to-point links have no election.
- Winner = highest interface priority (default 1, range 0 to 255). Tie = highest router ID. BOOK says this in one sentence; priority is set with ip ospf priority number.
- Priority 0 means: never become DR or BDR on this link.

- The election does not take over when a better router arrives later (it is not preemptive). The first routers up keep the jobs until the DR or BDR fails or OSPF is reset on the interface. CHECK (standard OSPF behaviour; not in the book)
- Routers that are neither DR nor BDR are DROther. DROther routers are adjacent (FULL) only with the DR and BDR. With each other they stay in the 2-WAY state, and that is normal.
MEMORY TIP
MEMORY TIP: Priority first, Router ID second. "PR" decides the DR.
OSPF neighbor states [ADDED]
| State | Plain meaning | If stuck here |
| Down | No Hello heard yet. | Interface down, passive, or wrong network statement. |
| Init | I heard your Hello, but you have not heard mine yet. | One-way traffic: ACL, or Hello settings problem. |
| 2-Way | We both see each other. DR/BDR is elected here. | Normal between two DROther routers. |
| ExStart | Deciding who sends database descriptions first (master/slave). | Often an MTU mismatch. |
| Exchange | Sending summaries of the database. | Often an MTU mismatch. |
| Loading | Asking for LSAs I am missing. | Lost LSAs, or very slow link. |
| Full | Databases are the same. Adjacency is complete. | This is the goal. |
VERIFY
The state list is from general OSPF knowledge, consistent with RFC 2328 but not re-read line by line in this session. The book only shows the words LOADING and FULL in log messages. CHECK
Quick check 6.1.1
Q1. Which table is the input to the SPF calculation?
Answer: The topology database (LSDB) - SPF runs on the LSAs stored there.
Q2. Priorities are all default. RIDs are 10.0.0.5 and 10.0.0.9 on the same Ethernet segment. Which is DR?
Answer: 10.0.0.9 - Priority ties, so the higher router ID wins.
Q3. Which of these can differ between two OSPF neighbors: area ID, Hello interval, router ID?
Answer: Router ID (it must differ) - Area ID and Hello interval must match; a duplicate router ID is a problem.
Q4. Two DROther routers on one LAN show 2-WAY with each other. Is that a fault?
Answer: No - DROther routers only become FULL with the DR and BDR.
6.1.2 OSPF Operation
OSPF works in three steps. BOOK p169
- Neighbor and adjacency formation: send Hellos, find neighbors, build adjacencies.
- LSA flooding: adjacent routers send LSAs so every router in the area has the same database.
- SPF tree calculation: each router builds a shortest-path tree with itself as the root and installs the best routes.
Hello and Dead timers
| Network type | Hello | Dead (4 x Hello) |
| Broadcast (Ethernet), point-to-point | 10 seconds | 40 seconds |
| Non-broadcast (NBMA), point-to-multipoint | 30 seconds | 120 seconds |

The book states the Hello times in the text and shows Hello 10, Dead 40 in a later output, but it never writes the Dead rule. The Dead interval is by default four times the Hello interval on Cisco IOS. ADDED These timers must match on both ends of a link. Sources for the defaults: secondary (see Sources table). CHECK
Multicast addresses [BOOK] [UPDATED]
| Address | Name (IANA) | Used for |
| 224.0.0.5 | AllSPFRouters | Hellos, and flooding between routers. All OSPF routers listen. |
| 224.0.0.6 | AllDRouters | Only the DR and BDR listen. A DROther sends its updates here. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Book Table 6.2 lists "Broadcast = 224.0.0.6" for updates. That is only half the story: on a broadcast link a DROther sends to 224.0.0.6 (the DR/BDR), and the DR then floods to 224.0.0.5. The two addresses were checked against the IANA registry (official). UPDATED
Cost: the OSPF metric [BOOK] p170

OSPF metric is cost. The cost of a path is the sum of the costs of the outgoing interfaces along the path. Cisco calculates the cost of an interface as reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth, where the default reference is 100 Mbps (10^8 bps). The result is at least 1. You can override it on an interface with ip ospf cost 1-65535.
| Link speed | Cost, ref 100 Mbps (default) | Cost, ref 1,000 Mbps | Cost, ref 10,000 Mbps |
| 10 Mbps Ethernet | 10 | 100 | 1000 |
| 100 Mbps FastEthernet | 1 | 10 | 100 |
WHY THIS MATTERS

Check with the book's own route. The book shows [110/65] for a route across a T1 serial link plus a FastEthernet LAN. Script check: serial cost 64 + FastEthernet cost 1 = 65. The numbers agree. BOOK p182
COMMON MISTAKE
The book says cost "is an arbitrary value as defined in RFC 2338". RFC 2338 is VRRP (and is now obsolete). OSPFv2 is RFC 2328. Both were confirmed on rfc-editor.org (official). UPDATED
WARNING

With the default reference of 100 Mbps, 1 Gbps and 10 Gbps links both cost 1 (the same as FastEthernet). OSPF then cannot tell fast from very fast. The fix is auto-cost reference-bandwidth under the OSPF process, set to the same value on every router. The book does not teach this. ADDED (Cisco's OSPF FAQ confirms the 100 Mbps default and the command; official.)
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Warning from the book (p171, and the multi-vendor story on p186): other vendors may calculate cost differently. If two routers assign different costs to one link, adjacency can still form but routing may behave badly. Match the cost on both ends.
Other things worth knowing [ADDED]
- OSPF has five packet types: Hello, Database Description, Link State Request, Link State Update and Link State Acknowledgment. It runs directly over IP (protocol number 89). CHECK
- LSA types (for later study): Type 1 Router, Type 2 Network, Type 3 Summary, Type 4 ASBR summary, Type 5 External. Single-area OSPF uses mainly types 1 and 2. CHECK
- OSPF routes show in the routing table as O (inside the area), O IA (other area), and O E1 / O E2 (external).
Quick check 6.1.2
Q1. A link is 100 Mbps and the reference bandwidth is the default. What is the OSPF cost?
Q2. A router has two paths to a network. Path A: costs 10 + 10. Path B: costs 15. Which is installed?
Answer: Path B (15) - Lowest total cost wins; A is 20.
Q3. Where does a DROther send its LSA updates on Ethernet?
Answer: 224.0.0.6 - Then the DR floods them to 224.0.0.5.
Q4. What is the default Dead interval when Hello is 10 seconds?
Answer: 40 seconds - Four times Hello.
Single-area OSPFv2 needs only two commands: start the process, then tell it which interfaces to run on and in which area. BOOK p171
6.2.1 Enabling OSPF
Start the OSPF process CHECK
Router(config)# router ospf 1
Router(config-router)#
- router ospf - starts the OSPF routing process.
- 1 - the process ID, a number from 1 to 65,535. It only separates OSPF processes on this one router. It is locally significant: it does not need to match on other routers.
COMMON MISTAKE

The book says the process ID "can't start at 0 because that's for the backbone". That mixes up two different numbers. The process ID has a range of 1 to 65,535. The area ID is a separate number, and area 0 is the backbone. They are unrelated. UPDATED
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says a second OSPF process "comes into play when you want OSPF to connect multiple ASs together". This is misleading. A second process keeps a separate database and does not share routes with the first unless you redistribute between them. For the exam, run one process per router, as the book also says. UPDATED CHECK
6.2.2 Configuring OSPF Areas
Basic network command BOOK p172
Router(config)# router ospf 1
Router(config-router)# network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0
- network 10.0.0.0 - an address to compare with the IP address of each interface.
- 0.255.255.255 - the wildcard mask. A 0 bit means: this bit must match. A 1 bit means: I do not care.
- area 0 - any interface that matches is placed in area 0. The area can be a decimal number (0 to 4,294,967,295) or dotted form. Area 0 and area 0.0.0.0 are the same.
WHY THIS MATTERS

What the network command really does. It does not "advertise the network you typed". It selects interfaces whose IP address falls inside the range. OSPF then runs on those interfaces and advertises each interface's own subnet. So network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0 turns on every interface that has a 10.x.x.x address. ADDED
Wildcard rule: block size minus one

The wildcard is the inverse of the subnet mask. In the interesting octet it equals block size - 1. A /28 has block size 16, so the wildcard is 15. A /30 has block size 4, so the wildcard is 3. BOOK p173
VERIFY
All values in the next two tables were calculated with the Python ipaddress module and match the book's own answers. ADDED
| Interface address | Subnet | Mask | Wildcard | Network statement |
| Subnet (book p173 example) | Block size | Wildcard |
EXAM CRITICAL

You must be able to look at an interface address and mask, work out the subnet and the wildcard, and write the network statement. The easy version network 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 also works in the book's example, but exam questions expect the exact-subnet version. BOOK pp173-175
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Another way (not in the book): turn OSPF on under the interface. Router(config-if)# ip ospf 1 area 0 places that one interface in area 0 without any network statement or wildcard. It is supported on current IOS, but confirm in your simulator version. ADDED CHECK
COMMON MISTAKE

Book review question 3 shows network 10.0.0.0 255.0.0.0 area 0. That uses a subnet mask where a wildcard mask is needed. This is a classic error. The book's answer: the wildcard mask is incorrect. How a real IOS version reacts to this exact line was not tested. CHECK
Quick check 6.2.1 and 6.2.2
Q1. Interface 172.16.4.9/22. Write the network statement that matches its whole subnet in area 0.
Answer: network 172.16.4.0 0.0.3.255 area 0 - Subnet is 172.16.4.0/22. Mask 255.255.252.0, wildcard 0.0.3.255 (script checked).
Q2. Which statement matches only the interface with address 10.1.1.1?
Answer: network 10.1.1.1 0.0.0.0 area 0 - A wildcard of all zeros means every bit must match.
Q3. Do two OSPF neighbors need the same process ID?
Answer: No - The process ID is only local to each router.
Answer: 0.0.0.31 - Block size 32, so 32 - 1 = 31 (script checked).
6.2.3 Configuring Our Network with OSPF

The book now builds a four-router network (Corp, SF, LA, Boulder) in area 0. OSPF has an administrative distance of 110. Before it adds OSPF, the book removes RIP with no router rip so the two protocols do not both run. BOOK pp175-178
MEMORY TIP
Good habit from the book: run show ip interface brief first on every router, so you type the exact addresses and avoid typos.
Book example, Corp router, with exact-address wildcards BOOK CHECK
Corp# show ip interface brief
Corp# configure terminal
Corp(config)# no router rip
Corp(config)# router ospf 132
Corp(config-router)# network 10.10.10.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
Corp(config-router)# network 172.16.10.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
Corp(config-router)# network 172.16.10.5 0.0.0.0 area 0
- no router rip - removes the RIP process (never leave two routing protocols running by accident).
- router ospf 132 - process ID 132. The number means nothing outside this router.
- network 10.10.10.1 0.0.0.0 area 0 - wildcard 0.0.0.0 means "exactly this address". Simple and safe, one line per interface.

The book also shows SF using process 300 and LA using process 100, with different wildcard styles on each router (exact address, /24, and a very wide 172.16.0.0 0.0.255.255). All of them work. Different process IDs on different routers is fine. When OSPF starts, you see a log message such as %OSPF-5-ADJCHG ... from LOADING to FULL, Loading Done. That is the adjacency becoming complete.
Passive interface [BOOK] p177
Stop OSPF Hellos on one interface CHECK
LA(config)# router ospf 100
LA(config-router)# passive-interface fastEthernet 0/1
- passive-interface fastEthernet 0/1 - OSPF will not send Hellos out that interface, so no neighbor can form there. Use it on LAN ports facing users.
- passive-interface default makes all interfaces passive; then no passive-interface name re-enables the ones you need. ADDED CHECK
- A passive interface that matches a network statement is still advertised as a network. It just forms no adjacency. ADDED CHECK
Advertising a default route [BOOK] p178
Book shows this with process 1 (see the error below) CHECK
Corp(config)# ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 Fa0/0
Corp(config)# router ospf 132
Corp(config-router)# default-information originate
- ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 ... - a static default route on the router that connects to the Internet.
- default-information originate - tells OSPF to give that default route to the other routers. It only works if this router already has a default route. Add always to advertise it regardless. ADDED
Book output on SF BOOK
SF# show ip route
- O*E2 - O means learned by OSPF, the asterisk marks a candidate default route, E2 means external type 2.
- [110/1] - administrative distance 110, metric 1. With E2, the metric stays the same as the route crosses the OSPF network (it does not add internal cost).
COMMON MISTAKE

Book inconsistency 1: Corp is configured as router ospf 132, but the default-route step types router ospf 1, and later outputs show "ospf 1". On a real router, router ospf 1 would create a second, empty process. Use the same process ID you already created. UPDATED

Book inconsistency 2: a static default route that names only an Ethernet interface (Fa0/0) is not best practice. Use the next-hop IP of the ISP router, for example ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 192.0.2.1. ADDED CHECK
WARNING
The book adds the Boulder router quickly with no passwords and says not to do this in real networks. Agreed. Never leave a router without console, enable and remote-access protection. BOOK p179
Quick check 6.2.3
Q1. What does O*E2 at the start of a route line tell you?
Answer: OSPF external type 2, and it is a candidate default route - O = OSPF, * = candidate default, E2 = external type 2.
Q2. What does passive-interface do on an OSPF interface?
Answer: Stops sending Hellos, so no neighbor forms on it - The subnet can still be advertised.
Q3. Which command makes OSPF advertise a default route to neighbors?
Answer: default-information originate - The router needs a default route first, unless you add always.
Q4. Administrative distance of OSPF, and of EIGRP (internal)?
Answer: 110 and 90 - Lower is better, so EIGRP wins if both offer the same route.

A loopback interface is a virtual interface. It is always up (as long as the router is running). The book recommends using it with OSPF for stability, as a management or test address, and for setting the router ID. BOOK p179
How the router ID is chosen [BOOK] [ADDED]
| Order | Rule |
| 1 (strongest) | The router-id command under the OSPF process. |
| 2 | The highest IP address on any loopback interface. |
| 3 (weakest) | The highest IP address on any active physical interface. |
VERIFY

Checked against a Cisco technical note (official): the highest address is used, a loopback wins if present, and the ID does not change until OSPF restarts or the router-id is changed by hand. The book gets the same result. The book's check on its own routers: Corp has 10.10.10.1, 172.16.10.1 and 172.16.10.5, so the highest is 172.16.10.5, which matches the book's "ID 172.16.10.5" (script checked). BOOK
EXAM CRITICAL

The router ID is used for the OSPF name of the router, for advertising routes, and as the tie-breaker in the DR/BDR election. Make it unique on every router. A duplicate router ID causes serious trouble. ADDED
6.3.1 Configuring Loopback Interfaces
Create a loopback with a /32 host mask BOOK p180 CHECK
Corp(config)# interface loopback 0
Corp(config-if)# ip address 172.31.1.1 255.255.255.255
- interface loopback 0 - creates the virtual interface Loopback0.
- ip address 172.31.1.1 255.255.255.255 - a /32 host mask. You can give every router its own /32 (172.31.1.1, .2, .3, .4) without using up a subnet per router.

A trap the book shows: after adding the loopback, show ip ospf still showed the old router ID. The router ID is picked only when the OSPF process starts. Three ways to apply a new one: reload the router, delete and re-create OSPF, or set it by hand and restart the process. The book chose a reload, then did it the better way: BOOK pp181-182
Set the router ID by hand, then restart the process BOOK CHECK
Corp(config)# router ospf 1
Corp(config-router)# router-id 223.255.255.254
Reload or use "clear ip ospf process" command, for this to take effect
Corp(config-router)# do clear ip ospf process
Reset ALL OSPF processes? [no]: yes
- router-id 223.255.255.254 - sets the router ID by hand. It beats every loopback and physical address.

- clear ip ospf process - restarts OSPF so the new ID is used. The book's log shows the neighbors going down and coming back up. This briefly breaks adjacencies. Do it in a maintenance window in a real network. ADDED
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says 223.255.255.254 was chosen as "the highest available IP address". It is the highest address in the old class A, B and C ranges, but there is no OSPF rule that says to pick it. A router ID is just a 32-bit number that must be unique. The usual real-world choice is the loopback 0 address, or a planned number such as 1.1.1.1 in a lab. UPDATED CHECK
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Book errors in the loopback section (p182): the book's show ip route output lists the loopback as 172.131.1.1 and repeats one line, but the loopback was configured as 172.31.1.1. These are typing errors in the book. UPDATED

Advertise the loopback or not? If you do not advertise it, other routers cannot ping it, but it does not use up real address space. The book suggests a private scheme (here 172.31.1.x). OSPF advertises a loopback as a /32 host route. BOOK CHECK
Quick check 6.3
Q1. A router has Lo0 = 10.9.9.9, Gi0/0 = 192.168.1.1 (up) and no router-id command. Which is the router ID?
Answer: 10.9.9.9 - A loopback beats a higher physical address.
Q2. You then add router-id 1.1.1.1. When does it take effect?
Answer: After OSPF restarts (clear ip ospf process) or a reload - The ID is chosen when the process starts.
Q3. Why use a /32 mask on loopbacks?
Answer: It is a host address, so each router needs no separate subnet - It saves address space.
Q4. Name the three router ID rules in order of strength.
Answer: router-id command, highest loopback, highest active physical interface - Strongest first.

Five show commands are the toolbox. The outputs below come from my own lab design (three routers R1, R2, R3 in a line, all in area 0, built in Lab 1). They are illustrative, not captured from a real run, so they are marked CHECK . Compare the layout with the book's outputs on pages 182 to 188. BOOK
| Command | What it tells you | Use it when |
| show ip route (or show ip route ospf) | Which routes OSPF installed (O codes), with AD 110 and cost | Is the route there? |
| show ip ospf | Process ID, router ID, areas, SPF run count | What is my router ID? |
| show ip ospf database | The LSAs: which routers and DR networks exist | Does my router see the whole map? |
| show ip ospf interface | Area, network type, cost, timers, DR/BDR, neighbor count | Why will this link not come up? |
| show ip ospf neighbor | Neighbors, their state (FULL, 2WAY), role and dead time | Are adjacencies formed? |
| show ip protocols | Router ID, networks per area, neighbor sources, AD | What is OSPF configured to do? |
EXAM CRITICAL
Read the routing table first. In [110/3], 110 is the administrative distance and 3 is the OSPF cost. This is exam objective v1.1 3.4 and v2.0 3.1 (interpret a routing table). ADDED
Illustrative output, R1 CHECK
R1# show ip route ospf
- O - route learned by OSPF inside the area.
- [110/3] - AD 110, total cost 3 (R1 Gi0/1 cost 1 + R2 Gi0/2 cost 1 + R3 LAN port cost 1, with the default reference bandwidth).
- via 10.0.12.2 - next hop, which is R2's address on the shared link.
6.4.1 The show ip ospf Command
Shows information for each OSPF process: router ID, number of areas, SPF statistics and timers. BOOK p183
Illustrative output, cut down CHECK
R2# show ip ospf
Routing Process "ospf 1" with ID 2.2.2.2
Number of areas in this router is 1. 1 normal 0 stub 0 nssa
Area BACKBONE(0)
Number of interfaces in this area is 3
SPF algorithm executed 5 times
- with ID 2.2.2.2 - the router ID. Check it first when two routers fight over a DR.
- Area BACKBONE(0) - the router has an area 0 interface.
- SPF algorithm executed 5 times - a high, climbing number points to an unstable link.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

The book's sample shows the router ID 223.255.255.254 and says it is "the highest IP address configured on the router". It is the router ID you set by hand with the router-id command, not a result of the highest-address rule. UPDATED
6.4.2 The show ip ospf database Command
Shows the topology database, grouped by area. The book says it lists the routers, not every link in the way EIGRP's topology table does. BOOK p184
Illustrative output. Age, Seq# and checksum values are made up CHECK
R2# show ip ospf database
OSPF Router with ID (2.2.2.2) (Process ID 1)
Router Link States (Area 0)
Link ID ADV Router Age Seq# Checksum Link count
Net Link States (Area 0)
Link ID ADV Router Age Seq# Checksum
- Router Link States - one line per router (a Type 1 LSA). Link ID and ADV Router are the router ID.
- Net Link States - one line per broadcast network that has a DR (a Type 2 LSA). The Link ID is the DR's interface address. The DR is the advertising router.
- If a router is missing from this list, it is not in your area map (adjacency or area problem).
6.4.3 The show ip ospf interface Command
Shows everything OSPF knows about interfaces. Use show ip ospf interface fa0/0 for one interface. BOOK p185
Illustrative output CHECK
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up
Internet Address 10.0.12.2/30, Area 0
Process ID 1, Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
Designated Router (ID) 2.2.2.2, Interface address 10.0.12.2
Backup Designated router (ID) 1.1.1.1, Interface address 10.0.12.1
Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
Neighbor Count is 1, Adjacent neighbor count is 1
- Area 0 and Process ID 1 - where the interface lives.
- Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1 - network type decides DR/BDR and timers.
- State DR, Priority 1 - this router's role on the link and its priority.

- Hello 10, Dead 40 - the timers that must match the neighbor. This is the answer to the book's question "what are the Hello and Dead timers by default?", which the book asks but never answers in words. UPDATED
COMMON MISTAKE
If you see %OSPF: OSPF not enabled on FastEthernet0/0, OSPF is running on the router but this interface did not match any network statement. Fix the network statement. BOOK p186
6.4.4 The show ip ospf neighbor Command
The most useful command in a real network. It lists each neighbor, its state and role. BOOK p186
Illustrative output CHECK
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
Neighbor ID Pri State Dead Time Address Interface
1.1.1.1 1 FULL/BDR 00:00:33 10.0.12.1 GigabitEthernet0/1
3.3.3.3 1 FULL/DR 00:00:36 10.0.23.2 GigabitEthernet0/2
- Neighbor ID - the neighbor's router ID (not necessarily an interface address).
- Pri - the neighbor's priority.
- FULL/BDR - state / the neighbor's role. FULL/DR, FULL/BDR, 2WAY/DROTHER, or FULL/ - (a dash means no DR/BDR on this link, for example point-to-point).
- Dead Time - counts down from 40 and resets with every Hello. If it reaches zero, the neighbor is dropped.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
The book shows serial links as FULL/ -. That is correct: serial point-to-point links do not elect a DR. The Ethernet link shows FULL/BDR or FULL/DR. BOOK

Multi-vendor story (p186-187): the admin fixed the Hello and Dead timers, but the link still failed, and the author then noticed the cost was different. In standard OSPF, a cost difference does not stop an adjacency from forming. Other causes (area, mask, MTU, network type, authentication) are more likely. Treat the cost part of the story as simplified. UPDATED CHECK
6.4.5 The show ip protocols Command
Works for any routing protocol. For OSPF it shows the process ID, router ID, area count, the networks you configured, and the sources of routes. BOOK p187
Illustrative output CHECK
R2# show ip protocols
Routing Protocol is "ospf 1"
Router ID 2.2.2.2
Number of areas in this router is 1. 1 normal 0 stub 0 nssa
Maximum path: 4
Routing for Networks:
Routing Information Sources:
Gateway Distance Last Update
Distance: (default is 110)
- Routing for Networks - your network statements (with wildcards) and their area. Check typos here.
- Maximum path: 4 - OSPF can install up to 4 equal-cost routes by default. CHECK
- Routing Information Sources - the router IDs of the other routers it hears from, with AD 110.
Other useful commands [ADDED] [CHECK]
- show ip ospf interface brief - one line per OSPF interface: area, IP, cost, state, neighbors. Quick overview.
- show running-config | section ospf - shows only the OSPF part of the configuration.
- debug ip ospf adj and debug ip ospf hello - live view of adjacency problems. Use carefully on real routers (turn off with undebug all).
Quick check 6.4
Q1. Which command shows the router ID, area list and SPF run count?
Answer: show ip ospf - It is the process-level summary.
Q2. Which command shows Hello/Dead timers, DR and network type for one interface?
Answer: show ip ospf interface - Add the interface name for a single interface.
Q3. What does FULL/ - mean in the neighbor table?
Answer: Fully adjacent, and there is no DR/BDR on that link - Typical on point-to-point links.
Q4. A neighbor stays in 2WAY/DROTHER. Is it a problem?
Answer: Not if both routers are DROther on a broadcast link - Only the DR and BDR form FULL adjacencies with them.
The book has no troubleshooting section for this chapter, so this whole section is added. Use it with the show commands above. ADDED CHECK (not tested on hardware)
| Symptom | Likely cause | First check |
| No neighbor at all | Interface down, passive interface, network statement does not match, ACL blocks OSPF | show ip ospf interface brief; show ip protocols |
| Stuck in INIT | Traffic works one way only (ACL, or the other side does not see my Hello) | show ip ospf neighbor on both routers; check ACLs |
| Neighbor never forms, no error | Hello/Dead timers differ, different area ID, different subnet or mask, authentication mismatch, stub flag mismatch | show ip ospf interface on both ends; compare |
| Stuck in EXSTART/EXCHANGE | MTU mismatch between the two ends | show interface and compare MTU on both ends |

| Adjacency FULL but no route | Network statement missing for the far LAN, or the far router has the LAN on a passive interface that did not match | show ip protocols; show ip ospf database |
| Wrong path chosen | Costs differ, or all fast links show cost 1 with the default reference bandwidth | show ip ospf interface; consider auto-cost reference-bandwidth |

| Default route missing on others | No default route on the origin router, or default-information originate was typed under the wrong process | show ip route 0.0.0.0 on the origin; show run \| section ospf |

Debugging order: 1. Is the interface up/up? 2. Is OSPF enabled on it (show ip ospf interface brief)? 3. Do both ends agree on area, timers, subnet? 4. Is the neighbor FULL? 5. Is the route in the table?

Subnets and usable hosts were calculated by script: 10.0.12.0/30 (hosts .1 and .2), 10.0.23.0/30 (hosts .1 and .2), 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.3.0/24. ADDED
Step 1: Addresses
R1 addressing. Repeat the same pattern on R2 and R3 using the table CHECK
R1(config)# interface loopback 0
R1(config-if)# ip address 1.1.1.1 255.255.255.255
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
- interface loopback 0 and the /32 mask - the router ID source and a test address.
- no shutdown - turns the interface on (router interfaces are off by default).
Expected result: show ip interface brief shows every interface up/up. ping 10.0.12.2 from R1 works (the first ping may time out while ARP resolves). CHECK
Step 2: OSPF on each router
R1 OSPF CHECK
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# router-id 1.1.1.1
R1(config-router)# network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

Expected result and why: the log shows %OSPF-5-ADJCHG ... from LOADING to FULL as each link forms. On R1, show ip route ospf shows O 192.168.3.0/24 [110/3]: three links of cost 1 (R1 Gi0/1, R2 Gi0/2, R3 Gi0/0). PC1 can ping PC3. CHECK Simulator route layout may differ.
Step 3: Verify (use all five commands)
Verification commands CHECK
R2# show ip ospf neighbor
R2# show ip ospf interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
R2# show ip protocols
R2# show ip ospf database
R1# show ip route ospf

Expected result and why: on the broadcast links R2 has the higher router ID than R1 (2.2.2.2 > 1.1.1.1), so R2 is DR and R1 is BDR on that link. On the R2-R3 link, R3 (3.3.3.3) is DR and R2 is BDR. (Election result checked by script, assuming equal priorities and routers starting together.) CHECK
Step 4: Make the R1-R2 link point-to-point (objective 3.4.b / 3.3.b)
Same command on both ends CHECK
R1(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
R1(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
R2(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
R2(config-if)# ip ospf network point-to-point
- ip ospf network point-to-point - treats the Ethernet link as a two-router link. No DR/BDR election, faster adjacency.
- Do it on both ends. A mismatch in network type on the two ends can cause odd behavior. CHECK
Expected result: show ip ospf neighbor on R2 now shows FULL/ - for R1. show ip ospf interface gigabitEthernet 0/1 shows Network Type POINT_TO_POINT. The R2-R3 link is unchanged. CHECK

Three routers, each with Gi0/0 connected to one switch, all in subnet 10.0.100.0/24: R1 10.0.100.1, R2 10.0.100.2, R3 10.0.100.3. Use router-id 1.1.1.1, 2.2.2.2 and 3.3.3.3, and network 10.0.100.0 0.0.0.255 area 0.
- Shut down Gi0/0 on all three routers. Configure OSPF. Then run no shutdown on all three at about the same time. (If one router starts earlier, it can win the election just by being first.)
- Run show ip ospf neighbor on R1. Expected: R3 is DR, R2 is BDR, and R1 is DROTHER. Script result: all priorities 1, so the highest router IDs win (3.3.3.3 DR, 2.2.2.2 BDR). CHECK
- On R1 enter ip ospf priority 100 on Gi0/0. Check again. Expected: nothing changes yet, because the election is not preemptive. CHECK

- Reset OSPF on all three (clear ip ospf process, or shut/no shut Gi0/0 together). Expected: R1 is now DR (priority 100), and R3 is BDR (router ID tie-break among priority-1 routers: 3.3.3.3 beats 2.2.2.2). CHECK
- On R3 enter ip ospf priority 0 and reset again. Expected: R3 is DROTHER and can never be DR or BDR; R1 is DR and R2 is BDR. CHECK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
